## 1. Purpose

This SOP establishes the physical documentation standards for
laboratory notebooks in the EA Program. A properly maintained notebook
is a legal record that establishes what was done, when, by whom, and
what was observed. These standards follow Good Documentation Practice
(GDP) principles used in regulated laboratories and ensure that EA
Program data are traceable, contemporaneous, and defensible.

This SOP covers *how* to record. For *what* to record during an
analytical session, see
[SOP-L802 Quality Control](SOP-L802-quality-control.qmd), Section 7.1.
For field notebook protocols, see
[SOP-F003 Field Notebook Protocols](../field_sops/SOP-F003-field-notebook-protocols.qmd).


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** All laboratory work performed under EA Program SOPs,
  including sample preparation, instrument operation, calibration,
  data reduction, and reagent/standard preparation.
- **Does not apply to:** Field notebooks (see SOP-F003) or purely
  electronic records in R scripts and Git (see
  [SOP-L801](SOP-L801-rstudio-github.qmd)), though electronic records
  should meet the same traceability standards.
- **Location:** All EA Program laboratories (SGM 133, 134, 135).


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role               | Responsibility                                         |
|:-------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI             | Set documentation standards; review notebooks          |
| Lab Manager        | Issue notebooks; maintain archive; verify compliance   |
| All Lab Personnel  | Maintain a notebook per this SOP                       |
| New Students       | Read this SOP before beginning any lab work            |


## 4. Notebook Selection

### 4.1 Required Type

Use a **bound, duplicate carbon-copy laboratory notebook** with
sequentially numbered pages. Each page produces an original (white) and
a carbon-copy duplicate (yellow). Acceptable examples:

- National Brand 43-648 (200 numbered pages, carbon duplicate)
- Boorum & Pease 09-900-2 series
- Any equivalent bound duplicate notebook with numbered pages

::: {.callout-important}
### Why Carbon-Copy Duplicates?
The duplicate page creates an instant backup that can be separated from
the notebook without destroying the original record. Duplicates are
filed separately, so that if a notebook is lost, damaged, or in use by
another researcher, the data are preserved. This is standard practice
in GLP, GMP, and patent-documentation environments.
:::

### 4.2 Unacceptable Notebooks

Do not use:

- Loose-leaf binders or spiral notebooks with perforated tear-out pages
- Composition books without numbered pages
- Unbound paper, sticky notes, or scrap paper
- Notebooks without duplicate (carbon-copy) pages

### 4.3 Issuing and Registering

1. The lab manager issues each new notebook and records the notebook
   number, researcher name, project, and date issued in the
   **Notebook Registry** (a spreadsheet maintained on the lab shared
   drive).
2. On the inside front cover, record: your name, contact information,
   project name, and the date the notebook was put into service.
3. Reserve the first two pages for a Table of Contents. Update the TOC
   as you fill the notebook.


## 5. Writing Instruments

### 5.1 Required

Write **all** entries in permanent, non-erasable ink. Use a ballpoint
pen that produces a clear impression on both the original and the
carbon-copy page. Black or dark blue ink is preferred.

### 5.2 Not Permitted

- Pencil (can be erased)
- Gel ink or felt-tip pens that do not transfer reliably to the carbon
  copy
- Erasable ink pens

::: {.callout-tip}
Test your pen on a spare carbon-copy page before starting a new
notebook. Press firmly enough to produce a legible duplicate, but not
so hard that you tear the paper.
:::


## 6. Entry Formatting

### 6.1 Every Entry Begins With

At the top of each new entry (or new day), record:

1. **Date** in ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD (e.g., 2026-05-18)
2. **Your name** (or initials, if your full name is on the inside cover
   and you are the sole user)
3. **Purpose** of the work session in one sentence (e.g., "TOC-L
   calibration and K~2~SO~4~ extract analysis, Project: BFS Soils")
4. **SOP(s) in use** with revision numbers

### 6.2 Contemporaneous Recording

Write entries **at the time the work is performed**, not from memory
afterward. If you record a result on a printout, sticky note, or scrap
paper during an urgent moment, tape or staple the original into the
notebook and initial and date it at the earliest opportunity. Never
discard the original note.

### 6.3 Level of Detail

Write enough detail so that another trained researcher could reproduce
your work using only the notebook and the referenced SOP. At minimum,
include all items listed in
[SOP-L802, Section 7.1](SOP-L802-quality-control.qmd).

### 6.4 Printouts, Graphs, and Attachments

Tape or staple instrument printouts, chromatograms, calibration reports,
or other documents directly into the notebook. Write across the border
of the attachment and the notebook page so that it is clear the
attachment was placed at that time. Initial and date each attachment.

### 6.5 Tables and Calculations

- Draw tables with a ruler if practical.
- Show all calculations, including units and intermediate steps, so
  that results can be verified.
- Circle or box final results for easy identification.

### 6.6 Blank Space and Unused Pages

- Do not leave large blank areas within an entry. If you finish an
  entry partway down a page, draw a diagonal line through the remaining
  blank space and initial and date it. This prevents later additions.
- Never skip pages. If you accidentally skip a page, draw a diagonal
  line through it, write "INTENTIONALLY LEFT BLANK," and initial and
  date it.


## 7. Signatures

### 7.1 Daily Signature

At the end of each work session (or at the end of each day if work
spans a full day), sign and date the last line of your entry:

> Signed: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_  Date: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

### 7.2 Witness Signature

For work that may be used in regulatory submissions, patent
applications, or formal reports, have a second person (the lab manager,
PI, or another trained researcher) review the entry, sign, and date it
as a witness:

> Witnessed and understood by: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_  Date: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

The witness confirms that the entry is legible, clear, and appears
complete. The witness does not need to have been present during the
work.

::: {.callout-note}
For routine student projects, a daily signature by the researcher is
sufficient. Witness signatures are required for thesis work, externally
funded projects, and any data that may be submitted to regulatory
agencies.
:::


## 8. Error Corrections

Errors in a laboratory notebook are normal. The way you correct them
matters.

### 8.1 How to Correct

1. Draw a **single horizontal line** through the incorrect text so
   that the original remains legible.
2. Write the correct information nearby (above, below, or in the
   margin).
3. Initial and date the correction.
4. Optionally, add a brief reason (e.g., "wrong sample ID" or
   "calculation error").

### 8.2 What Not to Do

- Never erase, white-out, scribble over, or obliterate any entry.
- Never remove or tear out a page.
- Never use correction fluid (Wite-Out, Liquid Paper, etc.).
- Never write over existing text to change it.

::: {.callout-warning}
Obliterated entries raise questions about data integrity. Even if the
error was innocent, an unreadable original looks like a concealment.
A single-line strikethrough with initials and a date is always the
correct approach.
:::


## 9. Handling Duplicate (Carbon-Copy) Pages

1. After completing an entry and signing it, carefully tear out the
   yellow carbon-copy duplicate along the perforated edge.
2. Place the duplicate in the **Notebook Duplicates** folder for your
   project, organized by notebook number and date.
3. Duplicate pages are filed in the lab (SGM 133, designated cabinet).
4. Do not take duplicate pages home or discard them.

If you do not tear out duplicates daily, do so at least weekly. Do not
allow a large backlog of unremoved duplicate pages to accumulate, as
the carbon transfer quality can degrade over time.


## 10. Electronic Supplements

Many analyses produce electronic data files (Isodat exports, TOC-L
CSVs, R scripts, photographs). The notebook must reference these files:

- Record the file name, storage location, and date for every electronic
  file associated with an entry.
- Example: "Raw data exported to
  `lab_data/BFS_Soils/2026/TOC-L/raw/20260518_BFS_run01.csv`"
- Electronic files are managed per
  [SOP-L802, Section 7.2](SOP-L802-quality-control.qmd) and
  [SOP-L801](SOP-L801-rstudio-github.qmd).

The notebook is the master index; electronic files are supplements. If
there is ever a conflict between the notebook and an electronic record,
investigate and resolve the discrepancy (do not simply overwrite one
with the other).


## 11. Notebook Completion and Archiving

1. When a notebook is full, record the date range on the front cover
   and spine (e.g., "2026-01 to 2026-08").
2. Update the Table of Contents on the first two pages.
3. File the completed notebook in the **Notebook Archive** (SGM 133,
   labeled shelf), organized by project and date.
4. Update the Notebook Registry spreadsheet with the completion date.
5. Notebooks are retained for a minimum of **7 years** after the end
   of the associated project, or longer if required by a funding
   agency, IRB, or regulatory body.
6. Notebooks are the property of the EA Program and Pomona College.
   They must not be taken home, discarded, or removed from the archive
   without PI approval.


## 12. Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                  | Consequence                              |
|:-----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Using pencil                             | Entries can be erased; not a permanent record |
| Recording data on scratch paper first    | Scratch paper gets lost; transcription adds errors |
| Leaving entries unsigned                 | Cannot confirm who performed the work    |
| Leaving blank space without striking through | Appearance that data could be inserted later |
| Using white-out or scribbling over errors | Raises data integrity concerns           |
| Not removing carbon-copy duplicates      | Backup is only useful if stored separately |
| Forgetting to reference electronic files | Data become disconnected from context    |
| Skipping the Table of Contents           | Information is hard to locate later      |

## 15. Training Record

Before beginning independent laboratory work, all personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Set up a new notebook correctly (inside cover, Table of Contents,
   registry entry)
3. Demonstrate a properly formatted entry including: header, data
   recording, attached printout, error correction, blank-space
   management, and signature
4. Be signed off by the lab manager or PI
